newsitem.title: UK: Demand for silver is brisk yet prices sag - study.
newsitem.headline: Demand for silver is brisk yet prices sag - study.

text.p: Strong demand for silver in jewellery in India and Mexico and higher use of it in photography led to stocks of the metal being drawn down to meet demand in 1996 for the eighth year running, an authoritative report said.

But the latest World Silver Survey by Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS), a leading precious metals research group, which was commissioned by the Silver Institute, noted that brisk demand and declining stocks were hardly reflected in prices.

Total identifiable stocks of silver have fallen by 540 million ounces since the end of 1990, compared with the cumulative supply/demand gap between 1991-1996 of 800 million ounces, according to the report released on Wednesday.
"While the...developments point to an improvement in silver's fundamentals last year, there was little evidence from the price to suggest that investors were returning to the silver market," it said.
After reaching a high of $5.86 an ounce in February 1996, the silver price slid for most of the year. It spiked up this March but could not sustain the momentum, returning below $5.00.
Among reasons for the sluggish price were the way that silver is linked in speculators' minds with gold, which is also weak, and a firm dollar.
GFMS said mine supply and scrap recycling rose modestly in 1996, but fell short of meeting the fabrication demand which grew to 803 million ounces from 769 million ounces.
Global mine output rose for the second consecutive year by three percent to 493 million. Out of this total 17 percent was generated by primary silver mines.
The largest producer, Mexico, raised output to 81 million ounces and modest increases were recorded in the United States, Chile and Peru
The gap between supply and fabrication demand had widened 13 percent requiring a 160 million ounce stock drawdown.

"Stocks of silver bullion are being steadily transformed into fabricated products which range from jewellery and tableware to photographic film and everyday consumer appliances," said John Simko, president of the Silver Institute.
Photographic sector use increased 1.4 percent to 226 million ounces while industrial demand was flat at 293 million ounces

The United States was the largest user of silver consuming 151 million ounces. It raised consumption for the fifth straight year on the back of economic expansion and more intensive use by sectors such as electrical contacts and brazing alloys.

India was the largest importer, spearheading the advance in global demand with 130 million ounces up from 99 million ounces in 1995. Bullion imports surged to 113.5 million ounces from 81 million ounces in 1995.
"A good monsoon last year produced bountiful harvests, particularly in the northern tribal belt where profits are used to purchase jewellery as a vehicle for savings," the World Silver Survey said.
Nearly all growth in global fabrication was due to higher production of jewellery and silverware. Demand in these sectors increased almost 17 percent to 263 million ounces.

"The evidence from...this survey suggests that the market is moving in the direction of a genuine tightening, with identifiable stocks now approximately equal to four years of the supply/demand gap recorded in 1996," the survey said.
Even so, the price remained largely unmoved. Silver was associated in investors' minds with declining gold prices, it said. The dollar's strength also wiped off any potential increase.
The survey said another key price issue was the rate at which the above-ground stocks of bullion and coins were being eroded by the excess of fabrication demand.
The absence of a price impact from the erosion of identifiable stocks suggested that there could be other substantial stocks which might have been shifted to fabrication.
But the survey argued that they were probably more "distant" from the market and required a higher price to mobilise them.

"If the existing holders of the remaining stocks of bullion should choose to maintain, rather than dispose of their holdings, then the only way that the market will achieve a balance...is via a significant increase in the silver price," it said.
